Enabling scalable approaches for the extraction of species occurrences data
and related data from historic scientific correspondence.
Legacy documents of various origin and purpose are a rich
source of biodiversity information.
For example, the reports from four meetings of the Berlin
Entomological Society, held from January to March
1915, detailed dozens of observations from
various taxonomic insect groups, some highlighted on these two example
pages from the report.
The accounts often featured detailed information on where and when the
specimens were found, remarks about noteworthy morphological or
physiological traits, and about the collectors of the specimens and their
collections.
As such, these sources are an invaluable and largely
untapped source of biodiversity data.
However, while the three basic information facets of
what was observed and where and when provide the basic pattern
of the accounts, the information is expressed in highly
variable linguistic forms, is often context-dependent,
and varies considerably in detail between accounts, as is
expected for natural language sources.
The overall goal of our project is to evaluate if and
how machine learning approaches can be used to extract occurrence and
related biodiversity data reliably,
at scale,
and in data formats suitable for computational knowledge engineering
As a first step towards this goal, we have assembled an annotated
reference text corpus of historical scientific correspondence.
The corpus consists of digital copies of the source documents,
manual annotations for reports of species occurrences in these written sources,
and a corresponding dataset of occurrence instances serialized in
RDF.
RDF structure is based on a conceptual data model that is aligned with the
annotation model and is aligned with the Darwin Core Standard and with
Wikidata and GBIF data schemas.
For the corpus, we concentrated on the journals issued by the Museum
für Naturkunde Berlin, the Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift,
Zoo Systematics and Evolution, and Fossil Record, and the
predecessors of these journals.
While the journals from their inception have been international journals, they
are expected to contain numerous references to objects contained in our
collection and to research based on our collection.
That makes these journals particularly relevant in the context of our collection
digitization and development.
To compile the corpus, we first identified bibliographic data
and sources for digital copies of the articles.
We then set out to harvest all available full texts, which
involved an iterative multi-step strategy with both automated
and manual approaches to deal with problem cases.
From the available full texts, a random, proportionally
stratified sample was chosen for further annotation.
In problem cases, which were not uncommon in articles originally published
before 1970, a new OCR layer was generated.
Note that for the Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift, and especially Zoo
Systematics and Evolution, the number of full texts that could be
obtained from both open access and access-restricted sources
is, for a number of reasons discovered in the process,
significantly lower than the number of articles published.
The tag set we developed for annotating a biological occurrence mentioned in
the text includes taxon, place,
date,
habitat,
quantity,
person,
and material to mark the text elements describing the
corresponding facets of the reported occurrence.
The occurrence itself, expressed by these semantically related text elements,
is anchored in the source text at the position of the first character of the taxon
name in question.
In our model, taxon names and at least one of the elements place and
date are regarded as strictly necessary for a valid occurrence report.
The tags implement the text-related part of the conceptual data model
that determines the characteristics of occurrences and reports of occurrences,
shown here in an overview.
Each of the tags can be mapped to a corresponding term in the Darwin
Core standard so that identified occurrences can be described using
Darwin Core terms.
In the first leg of our annotation campaign, we identified nearly
1,600 occurrence reports from 165 examined
journal articles.
Tag frequency falls roughly into three categories.
Places are reported in almost all instances.
Dates, persons, quantities, and materials are reported
roughly in a third of all instances, but not necessarily in the same
instances.
Information on habitats and about the location and identity of preserved
specimens using the org and ID tags is given in only
a small number of instances.
Annotations were created using the Inception platform.
The raw annotation data in the Inception-specific data format
is exported for subsequent standardization and enrichment of the
extracted occurrence records.
Specifically, the workflow attempts to match annotated
geographical place names with corresponding entities in Wikidata
over the Wikidata API. The matching was successful for
1,215 out of
1,333 place instances.
For the 681 distinct place entities identified in
Wikidata, the occurrence dataset was enriched with linked
geo-references and geographical context.
Similarly, annotated taxon names were matched to GBIF IDs.
The matching was successful for 1,041 out of
1,154 taxon instances. For the
741 distinct taxonomic entities identified in GBIF,
the data could be complemented with scientific taxon names, taxon rank,
and kingdom.
As a final step of the workflow, the extracted, normalized,
and enriched occurrence data is converted into a graph-based
serialization using RDF, RDF Schema, and related
data schemas. In summary, we have compiled a
comprehensive set of digital full texts for the journals issued by
Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde. It is complemented by a
manually annotated reference dataset of occurrence reports in a
sample from the overall full text collection.
The verbatim occurrence data is aligned and enriched with norm data,
is linked to the original text, and serialized in RDF
for versatile downstream data use.
Data structure is governed by a fit-for-purpose data and annotation model
that is fully aligned with the Darwin Core standard.
The workflow to obtain full texts and refine the data relies on a number
of scripts that can easily maintained and can be scaled and adapted for other
sources.
I would like to quickly address also a few of the challenges we encountered
and which are likely to be of concern in similar projects.
Document retrieval was indeed much more complicated than we had
anticipated in the beginning.
Different bibliographic databases hold different information on the journals
that is, in part, incompatible or incomplete.
To resolve these inconsistencies, it would help to have clear criteria
when a periodical is regarded as the same or as a different
publication by a bibliographic portal, and likewise for the links to
related journals like predecessors.
For this project, we relied on open access portals for historical texts,
in particular the Biodiversity Heritage Library, as well as
access-restricted repositories to ensure we get as much coverage of full
texts as possible.
However, even when using suitable text and data mining licenses, we
experienced erratic behavior of APIs operated by publisher
sites, which resulted in considerable additional work to retrieve full
texts.
When attempting to work with large sets of legacy documents, simple
access and download routes are clearly the more efficient option.
Annotating occurrences in the original sources has been challenging, not only
because it is very demanding to maintain consistent focus for a human annotator,
but also because of the large variability of linguistic forms used to express
occurrence information that has no clear boundary to other types of content,
like deliberations about the distribution of species.
Also, there are a number of knowledge gaps and semantic inconsistencies when
trying to interpret the verbatim information with respect to other structured data.
For example, matching historical place names to contemporary administrative units
accurately requires, in our experience, context and expert knowledge
that varies greatly case by case. We hope to build on this work
by extending the corpus quantitatively with more sources and
qualitatively with more entities and tags, and using the
corpus to evaluate and fine-tune AI-based relation
extraction workflows.
How could BHL support this kind of work further?
While there are probably very many kinds of relations that are in some way or other
expressed in the historic biodiversity literature, it would be great to
see entity recognition for entity types like persons or named
geographical places already being annotated and linked to norm
data, similar to taxon names.
Also, in the course of this project, we discovered that certain kinds of metadata
that link full texts, bibliographic details within one journal and
between related journals that are not yet included in BHL would be
helpful to discover sources more efficiently.
This work was, of course, a team effort and was made possible through support by
MFN's Innovation Fund. Thank you for your attention.
Thank you. Again, if you do have questions, please put them in the Whova app, and
Christian will answer them during this session, hopefully.
